example_sentences: I signed a one-year lease for my apartment.
Before you sign the lease, read the part about breaking it early — some buildings in Toronto charge two months' rent.
The tenant on the fourth floor pays rent on the first day of the month.
As a tenant, you have the right to ask for repairs in writing, and your landlord must answer within a reasonable time.
My landlord fixed the stove on Monday.
The landlord said the rent includes water but not hydro, so ask before you sign anything.
Utilities are not included in the rent.
When you move in, you usually set up utilities like hydro and gas in your own name.
The hydro bill was high last month because it was cold.
In Ontario, many people just say hydro when they mean their electricity bill — it comes from Niagara Falls power.
I paid a deposit before I got the keys.
The landlord kept part of the deposit because of the broken window, which is allowed if he explains it in writing.
The apartment is furnished — it has a bed, a sofa, and a table.
Furnished places cost more per month, but they save you from buying a couch and appliances in your first winter here.
Call maintenance if the sink is blocked.
The building sends a maintenance notice a week before they test the heating system every fall.
The superintendent lives in the basement apartment.
Neighbours just call him the super — he handles lockouts, garbage room problems, and small repairs.
My rent is due on the first of the month.
She sends her rent by e-transfer every month and keeps the confirmation email as proof.
She wants to sublet her room for the summer.
Most leases say you can only sublet with the landlord's written permission, so check your contract first.
The kitchen has all the appliances: a fridge, a stove, and a dishwasher.
Stores like Canadian Tire run appliance sales before Thanksgiving, which is when many families replace their old washers.
Turn the thermostat up if the apartment is cold.
Keep the thermostat around twenty degrees — cranking it higher wastes hydro and dries out the air.
I keep my winter tires in the storage locker downstairs.
There is usually a waitlist for the storage lockers in this building, so put your name down early.
My roommate and I share the grocery bill.
Having a roommate almost halves your rent in Vancouver, but agree on house rules before you move in.
The doctor gave me a prescription for my cough.
Your prescription has two refills, so you don't need to see the doctor again until December.
Ask the pharmacist how much medicine to take.
The pharmacist can check if two medicines are safe together — that service is free, no appointment needed.
A sore throat is a symptom of a cold.
Tell the nurse your symptoms in order — when they started, how bad they are, and what makes them worse.
You don't need an appointment at a walk-in clinic.
If you can't get in to see your family doctor, a walk-in clinic is the normal choice for minor problems.
Bring your health card to every doctor visit.
Each province has its own health card — an OHIP card from Ontario doesn't replace one from British Columbia.
My family doctor works near the plaza.
It can take months to find a family doctor who is taking new patients, so put your name on the provincial waitlist.
I have an appointment at ten o'clock.
If you cancel the appointment less than twenty-four hours ahead, some clinics charge a small fee.
The dosage is one tablet two times a day.
The label lists the dosage clearly, but ask the pharmacist if you're unsure about taking it with food.
I need a refill for my allergy pills.
You can request refills through the pharmacy app and pick them up after work the next day.
My work insurance pays for dental care.
Provincial insurance covers doctor visits, but dentists and prescription drugs often need private insurance.
I have an allergy to peanuts.
The clinic form asks about allergies to medications, which is different from food allergies like pollen in spring.
For a real emergency, go to the emergency room or call 911.
Emergency rooms treat the most serious cases first, so a small cut can mean waiting behind a heart patient.
I go for a check-up once a year.
Even if you feel fine, an annual check-up catches things like high blood pressure early.
You can get a flu shot at the pharmacy.
Flu shots are free in most provinces — pharmacies start advertising them as soon as October arrives.
My boss wants a sick note for two sick days.
Most Canadian employers don't ask for a sick note for a single day, only when you're off for a week or more.
Your paycheque goes into your chequing account.
Canadians spell it chequing with a q-u, and most everyday spending comes straight out of this account.
I move money to my savings account every month.
Keep an emergency fund in a savings account — enough to cover three months of rent and groceries.
Can I pay with my debit card?
Your debit card comes with a daily limit, so tell the bank if you're making a big purchase like furniture.
I pay this bill with a credit card.
Pay the full credit card balance each month and you'll build a strong credit history without paying interest.
I'll send you the money by e-transfer.
Interac e-transfer is how Canadians split rent or send money to a friend — you just need an email address.
There is a fee for withdrawals at other banks' machines.
Every withdrawal shows up on your statement instantly, which makes monthly budgeting much easier.
The savings account pays a little interest.
If you only pay the minimum on your credit card, the interest adds up faster than most people expect.
They got a mortgage to buy a house in Hamilton.
Newcomers can get a mortgage with as little as five percent down, but you'll also need mortgage insurance.
The nearest branch closes at five.
Open your account at the branch near your house — tellers there can help with anything complicated later.
Check your statement for charges you don't know.
A bank statement from the last three months is often accepted as proof of address for applications.
The teller helped me exchange money.
Don't confuse teller with tailor — one works at a bank, the other fixes your clothes.
Enter your PIN to pay.
Never share your PIN, not even with a bank employee — a real bank will never ask for it.
My account went into overdraft last week.
Ask the bank to decline the card instead of allowing overdraft — the fees are five dollars every time it triggers.
The exchange rate was good, so I sent money home.
Banks add a margin on top of the exchange rate, so compare a couple of apps before sending remittances.
You build credit history by paying your credit card on time.
Landlords in big cities sometimes check credit history, so start building yours early with a secured card.
We have a standup every morning at nine.
In the standup, share yesterday's work, today's plan, and any blockers — keep it under two minutes.
The deadline for the report is Friday.
If you can't meet a deadline, tell your manager early — Canadian workplaces expect a heads-up, not silence.
My blocker is waiting for data from the vendor.
Saying you have no blockers is completely normal — a blocker only means something you truly can't fix yourself.
My shift starts at three o'clock.
She picked up extra weekend shifts during the holiday rush to save for her parents' visit.
My paycheque comes every two weeks.
In Canada it's spelled paycheque with q-u, and most employers deposit it straight into your bank account.
Full-time workers get benefits like dental insurance.
Compare the benefits package, not just the salary — health coverage for your family can be worth thousands a year.
I get paid extra for overtime on weekends.
In most provinces, overtime means anything over forty-four hours a week and is paid at time and a half.
Send your résumé before Monday.
Canadian résumés are usually two pages and skip photos and age — employers can't legally ask for them.
I have a job interview tomorrow.
After the interview, a short thank-you email the same day leaves a strong, professional impression.
My colleague helped me with the new system.
Don't confuse colleague with college — your colleagues work beside you; college is where you studied.
Talk to your supervisor if the shift doesn't work.
A good supervisor would rather hear about a problem on Tuesday than discover it on Friday.
The work schedule is on the wall.
Canadians say schedule with a k sound — SKED-jool — which surprises speakers of British English.
New workers get two days of training.
Ask during training whether you'll be paid for the sessions — in most provinces, mandatory training must be paid.
She got a promotion after one year.
A promotion usually means more responsibility first and the raise conversation second, so negotiate both together.
I eat my lunch at the break room.
Most Canadian shifts include a thirty-minute unpaid lunch break plus a short paid coffee break.
You need a SIN before you can work.
It's called a SIN in Canada, not a social security number like in the United States — keep it private.
She became a permanent resident last year.
Permanent residents can live and work anywhere in Canada but cannot vote in federal elections.
After three years, she applied for citizenship.
The citizenship test covers history, symbols, and how parliament works — the study guide is free online.
My work permit is valid for two years.
Check the conditions on your work permit — some are tied to one employer, others are open.
Bring your passport to the appointment.
Renew your passport at least six months before it expires — many countries refuse short-validity passports.
The renewal of my licence was quick.
Start the renewal process early — work permit renewals can take months and expire-if-pending rules change.
I filled out the application online.
An incomplete application is the number one reason applications are returned, so check every field twice.
A bank letter works as proof of address.
For proof of address, officials usually want a utility bill or bank statement showing your name and current address.
The processing time is about six weeks.
Processing times change with the seasons — applications slow down before holidays, so apply early.
Bring the original and a certified copy.
A certified copy is a photocopy that a lawyer or notary stamps to say it matches the original document.
You can get a SIN at Service Canada.
Service Canada offices open early, and staff there serve you in English or French — take a number when you arrive.
Show two pieces of ID at the counter.
Pieces of ID usually means one government photo ID plus one more, like a bank card with your name.
My driver's licence expires in March.
In Canadian English, licence with a c is the noun and license with an s is the verb — a classic spelling trap.
Registration for the program closes Friday.
Bring your health card to registration day at the community centre — they'll photocopy it on the spot.
Check your eligibility before you apply.
The website has an eligibility checker — answering five questions saves you a long application for nothing.
Keep the receipt if you want to return it.
Don't confuse receipt with recipe — one proves you paid, the other tells you how to cook.
I asked for a refund for the broken lamp.
With the original receipt, most stores refund to your card within a couple of business days.
Can I exchange this shirt for a bigger size?
You can exchange it within thirty days as long as the tags are still on — that's standard at Canadian malls.
Students get a discount on Tuesdays.
Groceries rotate discounts weekly, so the yellow sticker aisle is worth a slow walk.
Call customer service about your bill.
Customer service will ask for your account number, so have your bill in hand before you dial.
The laptop has a one-year warranty.
Keep the warranty card and receipt together — one without the other won't get your appliance fixed for free.
The soup is on sale in this week's flyer.
Most grocery chains post their flyers online every Thursday, and the app matches them to your list.
There is no line at the self-checkout.
At self-checkout, the machine asks if you have your own bags so it doesn't charge you the plastic-bag fee.
We buy groceries on Sundays.
Grocery prices vary a lot between chains, so many families split their list between two stores.
Leave a tip for the server.
In restaurants, Canadians typically tip fifteen to twenty percent — the machine suggests amounts for you.
The fitting room is at the back.
Most stores limit you to six items in the fitting room, so bring your best picks first.
These winter boots are on sale.
On sale means a discount, but for sale means someone is selling it — mixing them up confuses clerks.
Delivery is free over fifty dollars.
Grocery delivery slots fill up before snowstorms — book the morning slot the night before.
Our internet plan costs sixty dollars a month.
Watch for the promotional price on internet plans — it jumps after the first year unless you call to renegotiate.
Restart the router if the internet is slow.
The technician will set up the router near the cable outlet — usually the living room wall.
My neighbour said hello this morning.
Canadians spell it neighbour with a u — a friendly wave goes a long way in apartment buildings.
We made small talk about the weather.
Small talk in Canada almost always starts with weather or weekend plans — short and friendly is perfect.
The weather is cold today.
Don't confuse weather with whether — one is rain and snow, the other introduces a choice.
We're going to a housewarming on Saturday.
At a Canadian housewarming, a small gift like candles or a plant is a thoughtful touch.

translations.hi: साझा भोज (हर कोई कुछ लाता है)

example_sentences: Bring a dish to the office potluck.
At a potluck, everyone brings one dish to share — bringing your own food culture's dish is always a hit.
She volunteers at the food bank.
Volunteering is one of the fastest ways to practise English and earn Canadian references at the same time.
The community centre has free English classes.
Community centres post their seasonal program guides at the library — skating lessons fill up in September.
We go hiking on the mountain every Sunday.
Join a hiking group if you're new — trail markers can be confusing, and groups know the easy routes first.
Tim Hortons is my favourite coffee shop.
Favourite keeps its u in Canadian English — ask someone their favourite double-double order and you'll fit right in.
Welcome to the neighbourhood!
When someone thanks you, reply you're welcome — or the very Canadian no problem.
